title: Testing Wayfinding in a Public Library
---
# Testing Wayfinding in a Public Library

A library can have accurate signs and still be difficult to navigate. First-time visitors do not know whether “services” means returns, accounts, printing, or research help, and a floor number says little about the route from the entrance.

## Give observers a real task

Ask a participant to return a book, find a quiet seat, and locate an accessible restroom. Record pauses, backtracking, questions, and doors they hesitate to open. Do not guide them after the first uncertainty; note what information they expected at that point.

## Change one decision point

A new directory at the entrance will not fix an ambiguous fork upstairs. Improve the earliest shared confusion, then repeat the task with another visitor. Include elevator sight lines, sign height, language, and lighting in the observation.

Quiet-space design is related but deserves a separate study of sound leakage, group zones, and user expectations. Keeping this route note self-contained makes it useful during a walk-through.
